Designing a Payment System (Stripe / Razorpay)

Simulate this design Draw it from memory

Difficulty: Advanced Topics: Payment Orchestration, Idempotency, Double-Entry Ledger, Settlement, Reconciliation, PCI Compliance Asked at: Google, Amazon, PhonePe, Razorpay, Stripe, Flipkart, Goldman Sachs Prerequisites:Message Queues, Database Transactions, and Scalability

1. Understanding the Problem

A payment system orchestrates the movement of money between buyers, merchants, and banks. It processes a payment request (card charge, Unified Payments Interface (UPI) transfer, wallet debit), routes it to the appropriate payment network, handles success and failure, settles funds to the merchant, and maintains a bulletproof ledger for auditing. The hard parts: exactly-once processing (never charge a customer twice), handling partial failures across multiple external systems (bank timeouts, network drops), and reconciling millions of transactions daily across banks that disagree with your records.💡 Exactly-once means a charge lands one time no matter how many times the request is sent or retried. It is the hardest guarantee in distributed systems because the network can always lose the *answer to a request that already succeeded. Learn more →*

Real examples: Stripe, Razorpay, PayPal, Square, Adyen.

2. Naive First Cut

Merchant calls API, API calls bank, returns success/failure.

Why this breaks:

  • Bank times out — did the charge go through? If you retry, you might double-charge
  • No record if the API crashes between calling the bank and responding to the merchant
  • No settlement — money sits in the payment processor’s account indefinitely
  • No reconciliation — disagreements between your ledger and the bank go undetected
  • No refund handling — partial refunds, chargebacks, disputes require complex state machines
  • No PCI compliance — raw card numbers stored in your DB is a security and legal disaster💡 PCI-DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard) is the card networks’ rulebook for anyone who handles card data. Every system that can reach a raw card number falls inside its audit scope, which is why the design works hard to keep that number out of our servers entirely.

The rest of the doc evolves this into an idempotent, ledger-based payment orchestration system with state machines, retry safety, and daily reconciliation.

3. Prior Art We’re Drawing From

  • Stripe Idempotency Keys - Every API request includes a client-generated idempotency key. The server stores the result of the first execution and returns it for any retry with the same key. This guarantees exactly-once semantics even with network failures. (Stripe Engineering)
  • Airbnb Payments Platform - Uses a double-entry ledger where every money movement is recorded as a debit+credit pair that sums to zero. Enables real-time reconciliation and audit trails. Processes $100B+ in yearly payments. (Airbnb Engineering)
  • Square Payment State Machine - Models each payment as a state machine (CREATED → AUTHORIZED → CAPTURED → SETTLED or FAILED/REFUNDED). Each transition is idempotent and persisted before side effects execute. Recovery after crashes replays from the last persisted state. (Square Engineering)
  • Razorpay Recon Engine - Daily reconciliation compares internal ledger with bank settlement files. Discrepancies trigger auto-correction for known patterns (timing differences) and manual review for unknowns. Handles millions of transactions with <0.01% unreconciled. (Razorpay Engineering)

4. Functional Requirements

Core (Top 3)

  1. Process a payment - accept a payment request (card, UPI, wallet), route to the correct payment network, and return success/failure with exactly-once guarantee
  2. Handle refunds and chargebacks - process full/partial refunds, handle bank-initiated chargebacks, maintain correct ledger state
  3. Settle funds to merchants - batch completed payments and transfer net amounts (minus fees) to merchant bank accounts daily

Below the Line

  • Multi-currency support
  • Subscription/recurring payments
  • Payment links and invoices
  • Dispute resolution workflow
  • PCI-DSS audit compliance

5. Non-Functional Requirements

Core

  • Correctness: Zero double-charges. Zero lost payments. Ledger balanced to the penny at all times.
  • Availability: 99.99% for payment acceptance (downtime = lost revenue for merchants)
  • Latency: Payment processing P95 (the latency 95% of requests beat) < 2 seconds (includes bank round-trip)💡 P95 is a tail measure: 95 of every 100 payments must complete inside 2 seconds. Most of that budget is spent waiting on a bank we do not control, which is why so little of it is ours to optimise.
  • Idempotency: Any request can be safely retried without side effects💡 Idempotency = running the same operation twice has the same effect as once. Essential for payment retries - charging a card twice would be catastrophic, and a dropped network response makes retries unavoidable.

Below the Line

  • Settlement within T+1 (next business day)
  • Reconciliation discrepancies < 0.01%
  • PCI-DSS Level 1 compliance (no raw card data in application tier)

6. Core Entities

  • Payment - a single money movement with a state machine (created → processing → succeeded/failed → settled/refunded)
  • LedgerEntry - an immutable debit or credit record (always in pairs that sum to zero)💡 This is double-entry bookkeeping, the accounting convention banks use: money never appears or vanishes, it only moves from one account to another, so each movement is written twice - taken off one account, added to another. If the two sides ever fail to cancel out, something is wrong, which is a check a single balance column cannot give you.
  • Merchant - a business account with bank details, fees, and settlement schedule
  • PaymentMethod - a tokenized reference to a card, UPI virtual payment address (VPA), or wallet (never a raw primary account number, or PAN)💡 The PAN is the long number printed on the card. A token is a meaningless stand-in for it that only the vault can map back, so our servers can charge the same card repeatedly without ever holding the digits.
  • Refund - a reversal of a payment (full or partial) with its own state machine
  • Settlement - a batch payout to a merchant covering multiple payments minus fees

7. API / System Interface

POST /v1/payments
Headers: Idempotency-Key: "order_123_attempt_1"
Body: {
  "amount": 1500,
  "currency": "INR",
  "payment_method": "pm_tok_visa_4242",
  "merchant_id": "m_456",
  "description": "Order #123"
}
Response:
{
  "payment_id": "pay_789",
  "status": "processing",
  "created_at": "2024-07-01T10:00:00Z"
}

POST /v1/payments/pay_789/refund
Headers: Idempotency-Key: "refund_order_123"
Body: {"amount": 500, "reason": "partial_return"}
Response: {"refund_id": "ref_101", "status": "processing"}

GET /v1/payments/pay_789
Response: {"payment_id": "pay_789", "status": "succeeded", "amount": 1500, ...}

Security notes: card tokenization happens client-side (Stripe.js, Razorpay SDK) — raw PAN never touches the payment server. All API calls over TLS with merchant API key authentication. Idempotency-Key is mandatory for all writes.

8. High-Level Design

FR1: Process a payment

A merchant sends us a card and an amount. We ask the bank for the money, and if the bank agrees, we record that the merchant is owed it. Read literally, that is one outbound call and one row.

Build that. A service, one bank gateway, and one Postgres table. The merchant’s running total lives in a balance column on their row. Everything else this page eventually needs — the idempotency contract, the double-entry ledger, gateway failover, the card vault — answers a non-functional requirement, so each is earned in a deep dive.

New components we need:

  1. Payment API - authenticates the merchant and validates the request.
  2. Payment Service - writes the payment row, calls the bank, records the outcome.
  3. Bank Gateway (external) - the card network or acquiring bank that actually moves money. We do not control it and cannot see inside it.
  4. Postgres - a payments row per attempt, and a merchants row carrying balance.

Flow:

  1. Merchant posts the card details and an amount of ₹1500
  2. The Payment API checks the merchant’s credentials and that the amount is well-formed
  3. The Payment Service calls the bank gateway and waits — this is the slow step, and it is most of the 2-second P95 budget
  4. The bank approves
  5. The service inserts a payments row with status = SUCCEEDED and adds ₹1470 to the merchant’s balance, after the 2% platform fee
  6. It returns the payment id to the merchant

Why call the bank synchronously instead of queuing the charge? Because the merchant is holding a customer at a checkout screen and needs a yes or no now. An asynchronous charge would mean telling the merchant “we will let you know”, which is not something they can show a shopper. The latency budget is 2 seconds precisely because a bank round trip is unavoidable.

What we have deliberately left broken. This takes money and records it, and every one of its shortcuts is the kind that ends up in a regulator’s report:

  • A retry charges the customer twice. If the merchant’s connection drops after step 3 and they resend the request, we have no way to recognise it as the same intent, so we charge the card again. Network failures are routine, so this is not an edge case but a scheduled one. That is Deep Dive 1.
  • balance is a number with no explanation. A column that gets added to cannot answer “where did this figure come from”, so a discrepancy has no audit trail and an off-by-one is undetectable. Money systems are required to be explicable, not just correct. That is Deep Dive 2.
  • One gateway means one outage takes all revenue. Step 3 has a single provider. When it degrades, every payment on the platform fails at once, against a 99.99% availability target on exactly this path. That is Deep Dive 4.
  • We are holding raw card numbers. Step 5 writes the card into our own database, which puts every server that can reach it inside PCI-DSS scope and makes one breach an existential event. That is Deep Dive 5.

FR2: Handle refunds

A refund reverses a payment — but partially and asynchronously. It has its own state machine.

New components we need: none. A refund is another row and another call to the same gateway.

New components: none, but the diagram above labels three boxes by the names these responsibilities take later in the page, so they are worth naming now:

  • Payment Orchestrator: the Payment Service in its coordinating role — it owns the order of steps (validate, write the row, call the gateway, record the outcome) so no caller has to sequence them.
  • Payment Router: the part that chooses which gateway to send a charge or refund to. There is only one gateway at this stage, so it does nothing yet; Deep Dive 4 is where having a choice starts to matter.
  • Ledger: the record of money movements that Deep Dive 2 earns. FR1 and FR2 still have only the merchant’s balance column, which is exactly the shortcoming Deep Dive 2 is about.

Flow:

  1. Merchant requests a refund of ₹500 against a ₹1500 payment
  2. The Payment Service checks the original payment is SUCCEEDED and that ₹500 does not exceed what is still refundable
  3. It writes a refunds row with status = PROCESSING and increments the payment’s refunded_amount
  4. It calls the bank to send the money back; the bank will take 5-10 business days to reach the customer’s statement
  5. It subtracts ₹500 from the merchant’s balance
  6. When the bank confirms, the refund row moves to SUCCEEDED

Why track refunded_amount on the payment rather than just summing the refunds? Because step 2 is a correctness check that runs on every request, and it has to be cheap and unambiguous. Keeping the running total next to the payment means the rule “never refund more than was charged” is a single comparison rather than an aggregate that could race with a concurrent refund.💡 Two refund requests arriving at the same moment can both read “₹1500 charged, ₹0 refunded” and both pass the check. The usual guard is optimistic concurrency: write the new total only if the row still holds the value you read, and make the loser retry.

What we have deliberately left broken. Refunds work and they inherit FR1’s wounds, sharper:

  • Step 4 and step 5 are not atomic. The bank refund and our balance decrement are separate operations across a network boundary, so a crash between them leaves the customer refunded while the merchant’s balance still shows the money, or the reverse. There is nothing to detect it. That is Deep Dive 3.
  • A retried refund refunds twice. Exactly FR1’s problem pointed the other way, and worse, because now we are giving away money rather than taking it. That is Deep Dive 1.
  • Chargebacks are missing entirely. A bank-initiated reversal arrives without us asking, days later, and this design has no path for money moving backwards that we did not start. Deep Dive 3 is where the states that can arrive from outside get modelled.💡 A chargeback is a refund the cardholder’s own bank forces through, typically after a fraud or dispute claim. The awkward part for the design is that it is an inbound event: our system has to accept a state change it never requested.

FR3: Settlement

Daily, batch all successful payments for each merchant, deduct platform fees, and initiate bank transfer.

New components we need:

  1. Settlement Scheduler - a daily cron that starts the batch.💡 A cron is just a timer that runs a job on a schedule, here once a night. Nothing about settlement is triggered by a user request, which is exactly why it can be a batch job rather than part of the payment path.
  2. Settlement Engine - groups yesterday’s payments by merchant and works out what each is owed.
  3. Payout Service - sends the bank transfer.

Flow:

  1. The Scheduler runs at 2 AM
  2. The Engine reads every payment that reached SUCCEEDED in yesterday’s window
  3. It groups by merchant, sums the gross, and deducts the 2% platform fee
  4. It writes a settlements row with the merchant, gross, fee and net
  5. The Payout Service transfers the net to the merchant’s registered bank account
  6. On confirmation the settlement row is marked COMPLETED

Why settle in a daily batch rather than paying each payment straight through? Bank transfers cost a fixed fee each, so forwarding every ₹200 payment individually would spend a meaningful fraction of the platform’s margin on transfer fees. Batching also gives a natural window in which a refund can net off against a payment instead of becoming two opposite transfers.

What we have deliberately left broken. Merchants get paid, and we have no idea whether the figures are right:

  • Nothing is ever checked against the bank. Every number here comes from our own tables. If the bank settled an amount we did not expect, or did not settle one we did, this design will never find out — and it computes payouts from the unchecked figure, so an error becomes real money leaving the account. The requirements ask for discrepancies under 0.01%, which is unmeasurable without comparing against an outside source. That is Deep Dive 3.
  • Step 2’s window assumes the bank agrees with our clock. A payment we recorded at 23:59 may settle on the bank’s next day, so the same payment can be counted in the wrong batch or, if the window ever slips, twice. Deep Dive 3 is also where timing differences get classified rather than silently absorbed.

scroll →

Why Postgres over NoSQL for payments? ACID transactions are non-negotiable. A payment that deducted money from a customer but crashed before recording it in the ledger is unacceptable. Postgres gives serializable isolation, and the payment DB is not horizontally-scaled (it’s sharded by merchant_id, with each shard small enough for one Postgres instance).💡 ACID is the four-part promise a relational transaction makes - atomic (all of it happens or none of it), consistent, isolated from other transactions, and durable once committed. The one doing the work here is atomicity: the payment row and both ledger entries land together or not at all.

10. Data Modeling

Postgres (Payment DB — payment state machine):

CREATE TABLE payments (
    payment_id UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    merchant_id UUID NOT NULL,
    amount DECIMAL(12,2) NOT NULL,
    currency VARCHAR(3) NOT NULL,
    status VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,  -- CREATED, PROCESSING, SUCCEEDED, FAILED, REFUNDED
    payment_method VARCHAR(20),   -- card, upi, wallet
    idempotency_key VARCHAR(64) UNIQUE,
    gateway_ref VARCHAR(128),
    created_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
    updated_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL
);
CREATE INDEX idx_payments_merchant ON payments(merchant_id, created_at DESC);
CREATE INDEX idx_payments_status ON payments(status) WHERE status = 'PROCESSING';
SQL

Postgres (Ledger — double-entry accounting, append-only):

CREATE TABLE ledger_entries (
    entry_id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    payment_id UUID NOT NULL,
    account_id UUID NOT NULL,       -- merchant_receivable, platform_fee, tax_collected, etc.
    entry_type VARCHAR(6) NOT NULL, -- DEBIT or CREDIT
    amount DECIMAL(12,2) NOT NULL,
    created_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
-- Invariant: SUM(DEBIT) = SUM(CREDIT) for every payment_id (balanced to zero)
SQL

Redis (Idempotency Store — prevent double-charges):

Key: "idem:{merchantId}:{idempotencyKey}" → Hash { payment_id, status, response_json }
TTL: 24 hours

Access Patterns:

Query Data Source How
Process payment (create) Postgres INSERT INTO payments with idempotency_key UNIQUE constraint
Check idempotency (fast path) Redis GET idem:{merchantId}:{key} → if exists, return cached response
Update payment state Postgres UPDATE payments SET status = ? WHERE payment_id = ? AND status = ? (optimistic lock on state)
Record ledger entries Postgres INSERT INTO ledger_entries (2+ rows, DEBIT+CREDIT pair, in same txn as payment update)
Daily settlement batch Postgres SELECT merchant_id, SUM(amount) FROM payments WHERE status='SUCCEEDED' AND settled=false GROUP BY merchant_id
scroll →

How Double-Charge Is Prevented with Idempotency Keys:

  1. Merchant sends POST /v1/payments with header Idempotency-Key: abc-123
  2. Payment Service checks Redis: GET idem:{merchantId}:abc-123 — if found, return the cached response immediately (no bank call)
  3. If not found: check Postgres payments.idempotency_key unique constraint as fallback (Redis may have evicted)
  4. If truly new: insert payment row with status=CREATED, set Redis key with NX flag💡 NX means “set only if this key does not already exist” - the write succeeds for exactly one caller and fails for everyone else. That makes claiming an idempotency key a single indivisible step rather than a check followed by a write that two requests could interleave.
  5. Call bank gateway. On success: update status=SUCCEEDED, write ledger entries (debit customer + credit merchant), update Redis cache with final response
  6. On timeout/unknown: status stays PROCESSING. A reconciliation worker re-checks with the bank after 5 minutes
  7. On retry (network glitch): same idempotency key → Redis returns cached result. Customer is never charged twice.

11. Deep Dives

1) The merchant’s connection drops mid-charge and they resend. How do we not charge twice?

Bad: What FR1 built — nothing distinguishes a retry from a new payment. The merchant’s request carries no identifier for the intent, so when their connection drops after we have already called the bank, their retry looks like a second customer buying a second thing and we charge the card again. The failure is guaranteed rather than unlucky: timeouts are a normal operating condition, and every well-behaved client retries them. It is also invisible to us at the time, because from our side both requests were valid and both succeeded. We find out from the cardholder, which means a chargeback and a dispute we will lose.

What FR1 built — nothing distinguishes a retry from a new payment. The merchant’s request carries no identifier for the , so when their connection drops after we have already called the bank, their retry looks like a second customer buying a second thing and we charge the card again. The failure is guaranteed rather than unlucky: timeouts are a normal operating condition, and every well-behaved client retries them. It is also invisible to us at the time, because from our side both requests were valid and both succeeded. We find out from the cardholder, which means a chargeback and a dispute we will lose.

Idempotency key stored in Redis. Before processing, check if key exists. If yes, return cached result. Problem: if the server crashes AFTER charging the bank but BEFORE storing in Redis, the retry will charge again.

Write the payment record (with idempotency key) to Postgres FIRST in status=CREATED. Then call the bank. If the server crashes after the bank charge, the payment record exists. On retry, the API finds the record, sees status=PROCESSING, and queries the bank for status (instead of re-charging). The idempotency key is part of the DB record, not a separate cache — it’s crash-safe.

2) The balance column says a merchant is owed 40 lakh. How do we prove it?

Bad: What FR1 built — a balance column that payments add to and refunds subtract from. The number may even be right, and it is unfalsifiable, which for money is the same as being wrong. Asked why a merchant is owed ₹40,00,000 the only answer available is “because that is what the column says”. There is no way to reconstruct how it got there, so an off-by-one from a retried update is undetectable and permanent, and a disputed figure cannot be argued either way. It also cannot answer the questions the business actually asks — how much of that is fees, how much is held against pending refunds, what did we owe on Tuesday — because a single mutable number keeps no history and distinguishes no categories of money.

What FR1 built — a column that payments add to and refunds subtract from. The number may even be right, and it is unfalsifiable, which for money is the same as being wrong. Asked why a merchant is owed ₹40,00,000 the only answer available is “because that is what the column says”. There is no way to reconstruct how it got there, so an off-by-one from a retried update is undetectable and permanent, and a disputed figure cannot be argued either way. It also cannot answer the questions the business actually asks — how much of that is fees, how much is held against pending refunds, what did we owe on Tuesday — because a single mutable number keeps no history and distinguishes no categories of money.

Event log of all transactions. Balances computed by summing the log. Correct but slow for balance queries at scale.

where every money movement records exactly two entries (a debit and a credit) that sum to zero. Account balances are materialized views over the journal. The invariant “sum of all entries = 0” is checked continuously — any violation means a bug. This is how banks work. Airbnb processes $100B+/year on this model. The ledger is append-only (entries are never edited or deleted — corrections are new counter-entries).

3) Every number we pay out comes from our own tables. What if the bank disagrees?

Bad: What FR3 built — compute settlement from our own records and pay out on that basis. Our tables record what we believe happened, and the bank records what did. Those diverge routinely and for mundane reasons: a charge we recorded as approved that the bank later reversed, a settlement landing a day late, a fee taken that we did not model. None of it is malicious and all of it is invisible here, because nothing in the design ever compares the two. The gap compounds, and since FR3 pays merchants from the unchecked figure, a divergence is not a reporting error but real money leaving the account. It surfaces at the worst possible moment — an audit, or a merchant who has reconciled their own books and can prove we are wrong.

What FR3 built — compute settlement from our own records and pay out on that basis. Our tables record what we happened, and the bank records what did. Those diverge routinely and for mundane reasons: a charge we recorded as approved that the bank later reversed, a settlement landing a day late, a fee taken that we did not model. None of it is malicious and all of it is invisible here, because nothing in the design ever compares the two. The gap compounds, and since FR3 pays merchants from the unchecked figure, a divergence is not a reporting error but real money leaving the account. It surfaces at the worst possible moment — an audit, or a merchant who has reconciled their own books and can prove we are wrong.

Daily : download bank settlement file, compare transaction-by-transaction against your ledger. Flag mismatches.

(borrowing from Razorpay): compare (1) your payment DB, (2) your ledger, (3) the bank settlement file. Discrepancies fall into known categories: timing differences (bank settled T+2 vs your T+1 expectation), currency rounding, bank fees not reflected. Auto-resolve known patterns; alert humans for unknown discrepancies. At scale, this runs as a batch job processing millions of records in minutes.

4) One gateway degrades and every payment on the platform fails. What then?

Bad: What FR1 built — a single gateway on the charge path. Its availability becomes our availability, and we are committed to 99.99% on payment acceptance while depending entirely on a third party who has made us no such promise. Total outages are the easy case, because at least they are obvious. The harder one is partial degradation: the gateway starts declining a fraction of otherwise-good cards, or its latency drifts past our 2-second budget, and every one of those looks to us like a customer whose payment failed. We have no second opinion to check against and no signal that the problem is ours to route around.

What FR1 built — a single gateway on the charge path. Its availability becomes our availability, and we are committed to 99.99% on payment acceptance while depending entirely on a third party who has made us no such promise. Total outages are the easy case, because at least they are obvious. The harder one is partial degradation: the gateway starts declining a fraction of otherwise-good cards, or its latency drifts past our 2-second budget, and every one of those looks to us like a customer whose payment failed. We have no second opinion to check against and no signal that the problem is ours to route around.

Multiple gateways with priority-based routing. If primary fails, retry on secondary.

Track real-time success rates per gateway, per card bank identification number (BIN), per bank. Route each payment to the gateway with the highest historical success rate for that specific card + bank combination. If Visa via Gateway A has 98% success but Gateway B has 92%, route to A. If A’s success rate drops below a threshold (gateway issue), automatically shift traffic to B within seconds. This 3-5% improvement in success rate translates directly to revenue.

5) We are storing raw card numbers. How do we get them out of our database?

Bad: What FR1 built — the card number lands in our payments table. Everything that can reach that database is now in PCI-DSS scope: application servers, backups, read replicas, log aggregation, the analytics job somebody wrote last quarter, and every engineer with production access. That is the full Level 1 audit burden, recurring annually, over a scope that grows every time someone adds a service. And the downside is not a fine. A single breach means every card we have ever processed is compromised, which is the kind of event a payments company does not continue trading after. The data is also of almost no use to us — we need to identify a card across repeat charges, not read its digits back.

What FR1 built — the card number lands in our table. Everything that can reach that database is now in PCI-DSS scope: application servers, backups, read replicas, log aggregation, the analytics job somebody wrote last quarter, and every engineer with production access. That is the full Level 1 audit burden, recurring annually, over a scope that grows every time someone adds a service. And the downside is not a fine. A single breach means every card we have ever processed is compromised, which is the kind of event a payments company does not continue trading after. The data is also of almost no use to us — we need to identify a card across repeat charges, not read its digits back.

Encrypt cards at rest with AES-256. Reduces risk but you still “touch” raw PANs — still full PCI scope.

Raw card data never enters your application servers. Client-side SDK (Stripe.js, Razorpay.js) sends the card directly to a PCI-compliant vault (separate network segment). The vault returns a token. Your servers only ever see tokens — never raw PANs. This reduces your PCI scope from SAQ-D (most complex) to SAQ-A (simplest). The vault is a separate, hardened service with its own audit boundary.

12. Design Self-Audit

  • Stale reads? Not applicable — payment state is always read from the primary DB (strong consistency required).
  • Single points of failure? Payment DB is the critical path — Postgres streaming replication with synchronous standby. Bank gateways are external single points of failure (SPOFs) mitigated by multi-gateway routing.💡 A synchronous standby is a second database that must confirm each write before the primary calls it committed. It costs latency on every payment and buys you a copy that cannot be behind when the primary dies.
  • Dead-letter / reconciliation? Payments stuck in UNKNOWN for > 24 hours go to a dead-letter queue (DLQ) for manual investigation. Daily reconciliation catches anything that slipped through.💡 A dead-letter queue is a parking area for items that automation could not resolve, so a payment of genuinely unknown status waits for a human instead of being guessed at.
  • Cost at scale? Bank gateway fees (2-3% per transaction) dominate. Infrastructure cost is small relative to transaction volume.
  • Exactly-once? Guaranteed by the persist-before-execute pattern + idempotency keys stored in the durable payment record.

13. Core Flows

Flow 1: Payment Processing (happy path + failure)

Non-obvious failure path: Bank timeout is the hardest case. The payment might have succeeded at the bank but the response was lost. The Orchestrator marks it UNKNOWN and schedules a polling job that queries the bank’s status API every 30 seconds for up to 24 hours. This eventually resolves to SUCCEEDED or FAILED without risking a double-charge (because we never retry the charge — we only check status).

14. Final Architecture

How it works end-to-end:

  1. Merchant initiates payment — API call hits the Payment API with amount, currency, and idempotency key
  2. Idempotency check — Idempotency Store rejects duplicate requests, returns cached result for retries
  3. Orchestrator coordinates flow — reads/writes Payment DB (Postgres), posts balanced entries to Double-Entry Ledger
  4. Payment Router selects rail — picks optimal Bank Gateway based on success rate, cost, and availability
  5. PCI Vault decrypts card — tokenized card data decrypted in the isolated vault, forwarded to the selected bank
  6. Bank processes charge — external gateway returns auth/decline; Orchestrator updates status
  7. Settlement Engine batches — end-of-day job nets transactions and posts final ledger entries
  8. Reconciliation Job verifies — compares internal ledger against bank statements, flags and fixes discrepancies
